claim: Neurons generate and propagate electrical pulses called action potentials which annihilate on arrival at the axon terminal.
source: Neurons generate and propagate electrical pulses called action potentials which annihilate on arrival at the axon terminal.
evidence: This is a fundamental statement about neuronal function presented in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: On annihilation, action potentials expel a local discharge.
source: We measure the extracellular electric field generated by propagating and annihilating action potentials and find that on annihilation, action potentials expel a local discharge.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' measurements of extracellular electric fields.

claim: The discharge at the axon terminal generates an inhomogeneous electric field that immediately influences target neurons and thus provokes ephaptic coupling.
source: The discharge at the axon terminal generates an inhomogeneous electric field that immediately influences target neurons and thus provokes ephaptic coupling.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study linking discharge to ephaptic coupling.

claim: The analytical model reveals excitation and inhibition in target neurons, depending on position and morphology of the source-target arrangement.
source: Our measurements are quantitatively verified by a powerful analytical model which reveals excitation and inhibition in target neurons, depending on position and morphology of the source-target arrangement.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analytical model simulations.

claim: The model is in full agreement with experimental findings on ephaptic coupling at the well-studied Basket cell-Purkinje cell synapse.
source: Our model is in full agreement with experimental findings on ephaptic coupling at the well-studied Basket cell-Purkinje cell synapse.
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' model predictions with existing experimental data.

claim: Less common in nervous systems of any organism are gap junctions between neurons, resulting in an aggregated functional unit because internal current is transferred from one neuron to the other neuron.
source: Less common in nervous systems of any organism are gap junctions between neurons, resulting in an aggregated functional unit because internal current is transferred from one neuron to the other neuron.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gap junctions in neural systems.

claim: The electrical field itself which is generated at an excited membrane can have an impact on the membrane potential of cells in the vicinity.
source: Beside these two forms of communication between neurons, the electrical field itself which is generated at an excited membrane can have an impact on the membrane potential of cells in the vicinity (Jefferys, 1995; Anastassiou and Koch, 2015; Rebollo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ephaptic interactions supported by citations.

claim: Rapid changes of the membrane potential, as it occurs when APs are generated, induce electrical fields, that by superposition are also present in neighboring cells.
source: Rapid changes of the membrane potential, as it occurs when APs are generated, induce electrical fields, that by superposition are also present in neighboring cells.
evidence: This is a statement based on established physical principles of electromagnetic field generation.

claim: The impact of a single, propagating AP on adjacent neurons is very small.
source: The impact of a single, propagating AP on adjacent neurons is very small, nevertheless, along active, parallel fibers synchronization of APs can occur (Katz and Schmitt, 1940).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Along active, parallel fibers synchronization of APs can occur.
source: The impact of a single, propagating AP on adjacent neurons is very small, nevertheless, along active, parallel fibers synchronization of APs can occur (Katz and Schmitt, 1940).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: When the term ephaptic interaction was coined by Arvanitaki, 1942, she concluded that the blockage of APs is the main source of such effects (hereafter ephaptic coupling) in nervous systems.
source: When the term ephaptic interaction was coined by Arvanitaki, 1942, she concluded that the blockage of APs is the main source of such effects (hereafter ephaptic coupling) in nervous systems.
evidence: This is a historical reference to the origin of the term ephaptic interaction.

claim: APs arriving at the synaptic terminal of a neuron annihilate, thereby generating a more potent electrical field for ephaptic coupling.
source: Indeed, APs arriving at the synaptic terminal of a neuron annihilate, thereby generating a more potent electrical field for ephaptic coupling.
evidence: This is a key assertion of the paper based on the authors' findings.

claim: The functional significance of ephaptic coupling at synaptic terminals is well documented in at least two systems: at the Mauthner cell in teleost fish and at the Purkinje fibers of the cerebellum in vertebrates.
source: The functional significance of ephaptic coupling at synaptic terminals is well documented in at least two systems: at the Mauthner cell in teleost fish and at the Purkinje fibers of the cerebellum in vertebrates (Furukawa and Furshpan, 1963; Blot and Barbour, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: In both systems, APs arriving at the synaptic terminal of the source neuron (e.g. the Basket cell of the cerebellum) modulate the initiation of an AP in the target neuron by transiently changing the membrane potential.
source: In both systems, APs arriving at the synaptic terminal of the source neuron (e.g. the Basket cell of the cerebellum) modulate the initiation of an AP in the target neuron by transiently changing the membrane potential.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of ephaptic coupling in these systems.

claim: Although the phenomenon of ephaptic coupling is known since many decades (Arvanitaki, 1942), a quantitative physical description is missing.
source: Although the phenomenon of ephaptic coupling is known since many decades (Arvanitaki, 1942), a quantitative physical description is missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that the authors aim to address.

claim: Ephaptic coupling at synaptic terminals is ubiquitous and may well contribute to communication between many different types of neurons, beside the mentioned Mauthner cell and Purkinje fiber.
source: This is even more surprising when considering that ephaptic coupling at synaptic terminals is ubiquitous and may well contribute to communication between many different types of neurons, beside the mentioned Mauthner cell and Purkinje fiber.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential widespread importance of ephaptic coupling.

claim: In 1952, Hodgkin-Huxley introduced a model (HH model) for generation and propagation of APs.
source: In 1952, Hodgkin-Huxley introduced a model (HH model) for generation and propagation of APs (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952).
evidence: This is a historical reference to the Hodgkin-Huxley model.

claim: The HH model is based on the cable equation and incorporates Nernst equations for different ions and changing ion-specific conductances upon activation of ion channels.
source: It is based on the cable equation and incorporates Nernst equations for different ions and changing ion-specific conductances upon activation of ion channels.
evidence: This is a description of the HH model based on established knowledge.

claim: The HH model is a powerful tool to study and evaluate the properties of ion channels in excitable membranes on a microscopic level.
source: The HH model is a powerful tool to study and evaluate the properties of ion channels in excitable membranes on a microscopic level, and the great attention it received since being introduced is more than justified (Catterall et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an assessment of the HH model's utility supported by a citation.

claim: The macroscopic phenomenon of current loops and associated electric fields is already well accounted for by a much simpler model introduced by Tasaki and Matsumoto (TM model) without the need of a multitude of specific parameters as required for example in the HH model.
source: However, the macroscopic phenomenon of current loops and associated electric fields is already well accounted for by a much simpler model introduced by Tasaki and Matsumoto (TM model) (Tasaki and Matsumoto, 2002; Tasaki, 2006) without the need of a multitude of specific parameters as required for example in the HH model.
evidence: This is a statement about the TM model's capabilities supported by citations.

claim: The TM model describes a resting and an excited state, each with a linear cable model.
source: The TM model describes a resting and an excited state, each with a linear cable model.
evidence: This is a description of the TM model structure.

claim: The TM model uses the cable equation with two state-specific parameters, its equilibrium potential and conductivity, which undergo a sudden (voltage-dependent) switch at the boundary between resting and excited state.
source: It uses the cable equation with two state-specific parameters, its equilibrium potential and conductivity, which undergo a sudden (voltage-dependent) switch at the boundary between resting and excited state.
evidence: This is a description of the TM model mechanism.

claim: The AP in the TM model has only 3 degrees of freedom, e.g., its propagation velocity, its amplitude, and its length.
source: The AP in the TM model has only 3 degrees of freedom, e.g., its propagation velocity, its amplitude, and its length.
evidence: This is a statement about the simplicity of the TM model.

claim: The TM model is well suited to describe the current distribution that is driven by the inhomogeneity of local electric fields in the internal and the external medium.
source: Nevertheless, the TM model is well suited to describe the current distribution that is driven by the inhomogeneity of local electric fields in the internal and the external medium.
evidence: This is an assertion about the TM model's applicability.

claim: The TM model is sufficient to describe the mutual influence of neurons by ephaptic coupling, using only three parameters for each neuron.
source: Thus, the TM model is already sufficient to describe the mutual influence of neurons by ephaptic coupling, using only three parameters for each neuron.
evidence: This is a key assertion of the paper about the TM model's utility.

claim: A suitable boundary condition (intracellular, axial current equals zero) can be generated experimentally by a collision of two counter-propagating APs.
source: A suitable boundary condition (intracellular, axial current equals zero) can be generated experimentally by a collision of two counter-propagating APs (Tasaki, 1949; Spach et al., 1971; Shrivastava, 2018; Shrivastava et al., 2018; Shrivastava et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations.

claim: Within any cable model, the very same boundary condition also exists within the axon at the synaptic terminal due to the broken translation symmetry for the current loops.
source: Within any cable model, the very same boundary condition also exists within the axon at the synaptic terminal due to the broken translation symmetry for the current loops (Spach and Kootsey, 1985).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about boundary conditions supported by a citation.

claim: APs do not penetrate each other but always annihilate at the collision site.
source: We observe that the APs do not penetrate each other but always annihilate at the collision site (Figure 1A; Tasaki, 1949).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The excellent fit of the TM model suggests that the discharge of annihilating APs is predominantly driven by the rapid depolarization at the onset of AP generation.
source: The excellent fit of the TM model suggests that the discharge of annihilating APs is predominantly driven by the rapid depolarization at the onset of AP generation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model fitting results.

claim: The failure of HH is in line with observations made in various studies, indicating that the rapidity of membrane dynamics is not well described by the HH model.
source: The failure of HH is in line with observations made in various studies, indicating that the rapidity of membrane dynamics is not well described by the HH model (Cole and Moore, 1960; Baranauskas and Martina, 2006; Naundorf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the HH model's limitations supported by citations.

claim: The general cable equation, linking field inhomogeneity to membrane current, applies to both source and target cell.
source: The general cable equation, linking field inhomogeneity to membrane current, applies to both source and target cell.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of the cable equation.

claim: The cable model directly explains why AP-induced membrane current in a neuron induces membrane current in targets.
source: The cable model directly explains why AP-induced membrane current in a neuron induces membrane current in targets (Durand, 2014; Merrill et al., 2005; Tung, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the explanatory power of the cable model supported by citations.

claim: Virtually all numerical computations of ephaptic coupling rely on the HH model which, as shown above, is not suitable to predict the effects caused by AP annihilation.
source: Surprisingly, this straightforward concept has never been applied to ephaptic coupling at synapses. Virtually all numerical computations of ephaptic coupling rely on the HH model which, as shown above, is not suitable to predict the effects caused by AP annihilation.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the literature based on the authors' findings.

claim: Electrical fields of propagating APs create positive and negative currents in equal amounts and a propagating AP first hyperpolarizes, then depolarizes a parallel aligned target neuron.
source: Electrical fields of propagating APs create positive and negative currents in equal amounts and a propagating AP first hyperpolarizes, then depolarizes a parallel aligned target neuron.
evidence: This is a statement about the effects of propagating APs based on the model.

claim: AP annihilation in the source neuron acts as a strong local current injection.
source: In contrast, AP annihilation in the source neuron acts as a strong local current injection.
evidence: This is a key finding from the authors' analysis.

claim: The nonzero discharge causes a more pronounced ephaptic coupling effect.
source: The nonzero discharge causes a more pronounced ephaptic coupling effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the authors' findings about discharge.

claim: In teleost fish, an interneuron with an axon cap can have inhibitory, ephaptic coupling on the Mauthner cell's AIS, where APs are initiated.
source: In teleost fish, an interneuron with an axon cap can have inhibitory, ephaptic coupling on the Mauthner cell's AIS, where APs are initiated (Korn and Faber, 1975; Korn and Faber, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ephaptic coupling in the Mauthner cell supported by citations.

claim: In the vertebrate cerebellum, the Basket cells show ephaptic coupling with the Purkinje cell, and the generation of APs at the AIS is inhibited by a fast gating mechanism.
source: In the vertebrate cerebellum, the Basket cells show ephaptic coupling with the Purkinje cell, and, comparably to the Mauthner cell, the generation of APs at the AIS is inhibited by a fast gating mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ephaptic coupling in the cerebellum.

claim: The cap structure (Pinceau or Basket) around the terminal of the Basket cell restricts local currents to the Purkinje cell, increasing its sensitivity at the AIS to extracellular potentials.
source: The cap structure (Pinceau or Basket; Ramón y Cajal, 1909) around the terminal of the Basket cell restricts local currents to the Purkinje cell, increasing its sensitivity at the AIS to extracellular potentials (Blot and Barbour, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Pinceau structure supported by citations.

claim: The TM model predicts a fast and strong inhibition when APs are annihilating at the Basket cell.
source: The TM model predicts a fast and strong inhibition when APs are annihilating at the Basket cell (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a prediction from the authors' model simulations.

claim: The magnitude of the delayed depolarization depends on the time course of AP repolarization at the source.
source: The magnitude of this depolarization depends on the time course of AP repolarization at the source (Figures 4C and 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' simulations.

claim: Presynaptic variation of AP width is a widespread mechanism for modulation of synaptic transmission by changing transmitter release.
source: Presynaptic variation of AP width is a widespread mechanism for modulation of synaptic transmission by changing transmitter release, and ephaptic coupling possibly contributes to a direct modulation at the postsynaptic neuron (Begum et al., 2016; Southan and Robertson, 1998; Kole et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, with speculation about ephaptic coupling's role.

claim: Blot and Barbour, 2014, described a biphasic modulation of Purkinje cells with delayed and synchronized APs in Purkinje cells after ephaptic inhibition by the Basket cells.
source: Blot and Barbour, 2014, described a biphasic modulation of Purkinje cells with delayed and synchronized APs in Purkinje cells after ephaptic inhibition by the Basket cells.
evidence: This is a reference to findings from a previous study.

claim: A biphasic modulation is consistent with the purely electrical framework provided in the RTM.
source: However, a biphasic modulation is consistent with the purely electrical framework provided in our RTM, and it remains to be investigated whether presynaptic modulation of AP width is the underlying mechanism for modulating the biphasic ephaptic coupling of Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of the RTM with experimental observations.

claim: Endogenous electric fields can influence molecular processes within cells, leading to cell growth, maturation, migration, and regeneration.
source: Endogenous electric fields can influence molecular processes within cells, leading to cell growth, maturation, migration, and regeneration (McCaig et al., 2000; Levin et al., 2017; Funk, 2015; Lyckman and Bittner, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge about electric field effects on cells supported by citations.

claim: The orientation of molecules and resulting structures can be induced by homogeneous electric fields and dielectric molecules can accumulate in field inhomogenities by dielectrophoresis.
source: The orientation of molecules and resulting structures can be induced by homogeneous electric fields and dielectric molecules can accumulate in field inhomogenities by dielectrophoresis (Cifra, 2012; Pokorný, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about electric field effects on molecules supported by citations.

claim: Such effects can lead to persistent structural changes in neurons and, thus, may contribute to neural plasticity and memory.
source: In principle, such effects can lead to persistent structural changes in neurons and, thus, may contribute to neural plasticity and memory.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of electric field effects.

claim: Prior, or in parallel, to chemical communication between the neurons that will subsequently form a synapse, Hebb's rule might be implemented by a discharge from the source and coincident activity in the target.
source: Prior, or in parallel, to chemical communication between the neurons that will subsequently form a synapse, Hebb's rule might be implemented by a discharge from the source and coincident activity in the target.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential mechanism for Hebbian learning.

claim: Ephaptic coupling might be instructive for synapse formation.
source: In this case, ephaptic coupling might be instructive for synapse formation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential role of ephaptic coupling.

claim: In the end-to-end synapse geometry with boutons, there is an initial sharp depolarization, followed by a slight hyperpolarization.
source: We included calculations on ephaptic coupling with the geometry of an end-to-end synapse and boutons on source/target (Figure 4C–E) and we find that there is an initial sharp depolarization, followed by a slight hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' model simulations.

claim: Ephaptic coupling is highly amplified when source and target neurons have boutons.
source: Ephaptic coupling is highly amplified when source and target neurons have boutons, and such a morphology is omnipresent in spines and also presynaptic terminals commonly have enlargements as well.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' simulations combined with anatomical knowledge.

claim: In the end-to-end geometry, depolarization can be expected about 1 µm away from the very tip of the target.
source: Our calculation further makes clear predictions where at the target (spine) depolarization can be expected, and this is the case about 1 µm away from the very tip of the target.
evidence: This is a specific prediction from the authors' model.

claim: Bidirectional propagation and hence collisions of APs might be more common than previously assumed.
source: Besides the annihilation of APs at the axon terminal, bidirectional propagation and hence collisions of APs might be more common than previously assumed (Mateus et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2007; Debanne et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential prevalence of AP collisions supported by citations.

claim: In theory, collisions can be used to perform computations.
source: In theory, collisions can be used to perform computations (Siccardi et al., 2016) and neural networks possibly also perform such kind of information processing.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential computational uses of collisions supported by a citation.

claim: Neurons for sound source localization perform a timing analysis based on binaural input.
source: For example, neurons for sound source localization perform a timing analysis based on binaural input.
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory processing.

claim: A neural network described as Jeffress delay line can accomplish sound source localization computation.
source: A neural network described as Jeffress delay line can accomplish such computation (Jeffress, 1948).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Jeffress model supported by a citation.

claim: Franken et al., 2021, performed a delay sweep experiment and their findings on integration at MSO neurons look intriguingly similar to the collision experiment.
source: Franken et al., 2021, performed a delay sweep experiment and their findings on integration at MSO neurons (medial superior olive neurons in vertebrates) look intriguingly similar to our collision experiment.
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' findings with another study.

claim: Ephaptic coupling is ubiquitous.
source: Irrespective of such speculative functionalities, ephaptic coupling is ubiquitous.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of ephaptic coupling.

claim: Ephaptic coupling effects span spectacular length and timescales, in some cases it can bridge up to hundreds of microns.
source: Its effects span spectacular length and timescales, in some cases it can bridge up to hundreds of microns (Kriebel, 1968; Chiang et al., 2019; Shivacharan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the spatial extent of ephaptic coupling supported by citations.

claim: The ventral nerve cord contains two giant fibers, the MGF and LGF.
source: The VNC contains two giant fibers, the MGF and LGF.
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about the earthworm nervous system.

claim: The MGF and LGF are unambiguously distinguished by their individual stimulation threshold and propagation velocity.
source: These are unambiguously distinguished by their individual stimulation threshold and propagation velocity.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how the fibers are identified.

claim: The TM model and the RTM allow the reconstruction of the extracellular field of propagating APs within satisfying accuracy.
source: All models allow the reconstruction of the extracellular field of propagating APs within satisfying accuracy.
evidence: This is an assessment of the model performance based on comparisons with experimental data.

claim: The HH model largely disagrees with the experiments both in the magnitude of the discharge and in its temporal shape.
source: On the other hand, the HH model largely disagrees with the experiments both in the magnitude of the discharge and in its temporal shape.
evidence: This is a comparison of the HH model predictions with experimental measurements.

claim: The modulation of activity in Purkinje cells in response to an AP arriving at the Pinceau of the Basket cell was described in detail by Blot and Barbour, 2014.
source: The modulation of activity in Purkinje cells, e.g., changes in the rate of APs in response to an AP arriving at the Pinceau of the Basket cell was described in detail by Blot and Barbour, 2014.
evidence: This is a reference to findings from a previous study.

claim: In the TM and RTM models, the modulation of not terminating but propagating APs along the source axon on the AP rate of the target cell is minute.
source: In our two models (TM and RTM), the modulation of not terminating but propagating APs along the source axon on the AP rate of the target cell is minute (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' model simulations.

claim: For annihilating APs at the axon terminal, with excitable segments up to the very end, the models reveal a moderate modulation, and only about half of what was reported for the Purkinje cell by Blot and Barbour, 2014.
source: For annihilating APs at the axon terminal, with excitable segments up to the very end, our models reveal a moderate modulation, and only about half of what was reported for the Purkinje cell by Blot and Barbour, 2014.
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with experimental data from the literature.

claim: At the Pinceau a different set of ion channels is expressed and it is considered as being non-excitable.
source: At the Pinceau a different set of ion channels is expressed and it is considered as being non-excitable (Laube et al., 1996; Southan and Robertson, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Pinceau structure supported by citations.

claim: The distant depolarization shown for the end-end synapse is only a few tens of µV, but as the amplitude of synchronized input from many dendrites adds up and cerebellar neurons have thousands of dendrites we may expect depolarization signal strengths in the mV range.
source: The distant depolarization shown for the end-end synapse (Figure 4D and E) is only a few tens of µV, but as the amplitude of synchronized input from many dendrites adds up and cerebellar neurons have thousands of dendrites we may expect depolarization signal strengths in the mV range.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential cumulative effect of ephaptic coupling from multiple inputs.

claim: AP propagation is terminated when the overall local axial current is annihilated by a collision event and at axon terminals.
source: In fact, AP propagation is terminated when the overall local axial current is annihilated by a collision event and at axon terminals.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of AP termination based on the model.

claim: During AP annihilation, the extracellular potential becomes a distinct monophasic spike.
source: During AP annihilation, the extracellular potential becomes a distinct monophasic spike.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: This phenomenon has been observed for artificially produced as well as naturally occurring collisions in various systems.
source: This phenomenon has been observed for artificially produced as well as naturally occurring collisions in various systems (Spach et al., 1971; Steinhaus et al., 1985; Tasaki, 1949; Tasaki, 1955).
evidence: This is a statement about the generality of the phenomenon supported by citations.

claim: The impact of extracellular potentials that are applied with microelectrodes is often described with the term 'activating function'.
source: The impact of extracellular potentials that are applied with microelectrodes is often described with the term 'activating function' (Rattay, 2008).
evidence: This is established terminology in the field supported by a citation.

claim: The rapidity of membrane dynamics is not well described by the HH model.
source: The failure of HH is in line with observations made in various studies, indicating that the rapidity of membrane dynamics is not well described by the HH model (Cole and Moore, 1960; Baranauskas and Martina, 2006; Naundorf et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the HH model supported by citations.
